utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 4th of March, 2010. I would like to welcome General Petkovic, first of all, the accused who are in the courtroom, Mr. Prlic, Coric, Stojic, and Pusic. I would like to welcome Defence counsel, Mr. Scott as well as all his associates, and all the people assisting us in this courtroom, and also the security guards. I have two oral decisions to hand down, which I shall hand down straight away. These are long. I believe too formal, but whatever the case may be, relating to the application by Stojic and Petkovic Defence teams to be granted additional time to cross-examine Witness 5D-AB. The Witness 5D-AB presented by the Coric Defence team will testify as a viva voce witness from the 12th to the 14th of April, 2010, according to the latest schedule that has been filed. The Coric Defence has informed the Chamber and the parties of its intention to have two hours for the examination-in-chief and redirect, if any, for the witness. In its motion on the 1st of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence asked to have one hour, i.e., an extra 48 minutes, as opposed to the time which would be allocated pursuant to Guide-line number 5 to cross-examine Witness 5D-AB. The Coric Defence team has responded to this on the 5th of February, 2010. The 9th of February, 2010, the Trial Chamber authorised the Petkovic Defence to file a reply, which it did on the 12th of February, 2010. After that, it was notified on the 10th of February, 2010, by the Stojic Defence, that requested an extra 20 minutes from the Chamber to cross-examine the witness. It requested, furthermore, that this additional time be taken off the overall time which had been allocated to it by the Chamber. After having looked at the 65 ter summary relating to the testimony of 5D-AB, the Trial Chamber holds that the additional time application filed by the Stojic Defence is founded and proportionate. The Trial Chamber, therefore, states that it can have 20 extra minutes to cross-examine the witness, which means that the overall time of its cross-examination will be 32 minutes. The Trial Chamber also notes that the Stojic Defence has requested to have 20 minutes' time taken off its overall time. As far as the application filed by the Petkovic Defence is concerned, the Trial Chamber feels that an extra hour to cross-examine is disproportionate, in light of the material in the 65 ter summary of Witness 5D-AB. The Trial Chamber holds that 30 minutes of extra time is enough to enable the counsel to protect the interests of their client, which means that the overall time of their cross-examination will be 42 minutes. Accordingly, time allocation will be broken down as follows: The Coric Defence will have two hours to conduct its examination-in-chief and redirect, if any. The Stojic Defence will have 32 minutes for its cross-examination. The Petkovic Defence will have 42 minutes for its cross-examination. In the absence of any specific application, the Prlic, Praljak and Pusic Defence teams will have 12 minutes each to cross-examine, if need be. And, lastly, the Prosecution, pursuant to Guide-line number 5, will have two hours for its cross-examination. I would like to say that this very long decision could have -- could read as follows: In light of the parties' submission, the Trial Chamber decides to allocate two hours to the Coric Defence team, 30 minutes to the Stojic Defence team, 40 minutes to the Petkovic Defence team, and 12 minutes each for the other Defence teams, and two hours to be allocated to the Prosecution. This is what I would have said, had I been on my own. Oral decision relating to the Prosecution's application, and Petkovic and Stojic Defence teams to have extra time to cross-examine the Witness Mate Jelcic, relating to the time allocated for the appearance of this witness. Please be patient. This going to take a long time. Witness Mate Jelcic presented by the Coric Defence team must come as a witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter of our Rules of the 24th of March, 2010. The Coric Defence team has informed the Trial Chamber and the parties that it intends to examine in-chief this witness for 30 minutes. In its motion -- confidential motion filed on the 1st of February, 2010, the Prosecution has asked to have two hours to cross-examine this witness. The Coric Defence responded to the motion on the 3rd of February, 2010. On the 3rd of February, 2010, also, the Praljak Defence joined in the response filed by the Coric Defence. On the 14th [as interpreted] of February, 2010, the Prosecution asked to be entitled to reply and to be entitled to reply to the -- and responded. Furthermore, the Petkovic Defence filed a confidential motion on the 4th of February, 2010, in which it asked to have 30 minutes to cross-examine Witness Mate Jelcic, i.e., an extra 18 minutes. On the 15th of February, 2010, the Coric Defence responded to the motion. The Trial Chamber authorises the Petkovic Defence to file a motion in its oral decision of the 16th of February, 2010. This reply was filed on the 17th of February, 2010. Lastly, the Stojic Defence team has filed a confidential motion on the 5th of February, 2010, in which it asks to have 24 minutes, i.e., an extra 12 minutes, to conduct the cross-examination of this witness. It asks, in addition, that the additional time that has been requested be taken off the overall time which was allocated to it by the Trial Chamber. The Coric Defence responded to the motion on the 15th of February, 2010. As a preliminary matter, the Trial Chamber decides to authorise the reply by the Prosecution filed on the 4th of February, 2010, as far as Witness Mate Jelcic is concerned. The Trial Chamber notes, furthermore, that this witness, initially on the 65 ter list of the Coric Defence, was listed as a viva voce witness, with an examination-in-chief lasting two hours. In light of the submissions presented by the parties, in light of the 65 ter summary of the witness, and the practices of the Chamber with regard to time allocation to cross-examine a witness that testifies pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules, the Trial Chamber has decided as follows: The Coric Defence will have, for its examination-in-chief and redirect, if any, 30 minutes. The Trial Chamber grants the request filed by the Prosecution and grants it two hours to cross-examine Witness Mate Jelcic. The Trial Chamber also decides to grant the Petkovic Defence application and to grant it, all in all, 30 minutes to conduct its cross-examination. Then, and in light of the sole topic addressed by the Stojic Defence, which intends to address with the witness of the Court, will have 20 minutes to entitle it to conduct its examination-in-chief. The Stojic Defence has asked the Trial Chamber to take this time off, i.e., eight minutes off its overall time. The Prlic, Praljak, Pusic Defence teams that have not filed any particular application will have 36 minutes each to be shared between them, if they wish to cross-examine this witness. This decision could have been read as follows, in light of the submissions presented by the parties: The Trial Chamber is to grant the Coric Defence 30 minutes, the Prosecution two hours, the Petkovic Defence 30 minutes, the Stojic Defence 20 minutes, and the other Defence teams 36 minutes. That said, those questions that haven't been planned will be taken off their overall time; i.e., eight minutes for the Stojic Defence. I hope everyone has understood. Mr. Scott, you have the floor, and I give you the floor with pleasure. You may start by continuing your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to all of Your Honours, and good afternoon to all of you, to counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Petkovic. Sir, I'd like to go back to -- and do a very small bit of review, based on where we left off yesterday. We were talking about the circumstances surrounding your being called to The Hague to testify in the Blaskic case. I had put to you, sir, that upon receiving information that you were going to be called, or at least were being considered to be called, that the Tudjman government was very concerned about this. They were very concerned about what you might say if you came to The Hague and gave testimony. And, in fact, they were concerned because -- and we'll see, I think, in a few minutes that they considered that you knew too much. You knew too much. It would be dangerous for you to come from [sic] The Hague, because things might come to light that the Tudjman government would prefer not to. And in the course of your conversations with the Tudjman government and its representatives about coming here, you knew that, didn't you? 3 A. No, Your Honours, I didn't know why they were concerned and how concerned 4 they were. I only knew that they had contact with the Tribunal, and I was standing aside, and I only heard about the outcome, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, as further review, before we move forward, if I can ask to -- in Sanction, if we can display slide 33, please. There's just a small -- a few items from your related testimony on this yesterday, sir. You had indicated that Mr. Rebic, Markica Rebic, who we've talked about before and which the Chamber, I think, has come to know, to some extent, that he never contacted you. Your evidence -- you said: "My evidence, as I said, had been agreed upon without anybody asking me anything about it." "No, Your Honour, nobody controlled that testimony," you said. "The Croatian government didn't influence me ..." "The Croatian government displayed no interest whatsoever in the contents of my evidence." Now, with that in mind, sir, I think in the course of the afternoon you mentioned the man -- the man Pavao -- or maybe it was morning, I suppose, Pavao Miljavac, Miljavac, excuse me. He was the Croatian minister of defence in April 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Miljavac was minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that sense or in that position, he was your superior at the time. And when you mentioned a couple of times yesterday talking to someone or getting permission, et cetera, you were talking, in particular, about Mr. Miljavac?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which permission I spoke about, but I said that Miljavac was the minister of defence of Croatia and that he had summoned me when the government had received the notification that I had to testify, and he handed me the summons, because the summons didn't come to me, personally; it was addressed to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a man named Kresimir Cosic was the deputy defence minister at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what position did the man named Davorin Domazet hold in the Croatian government or military in -- at the time of your summons or subpoena in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was Chief of Main Staff, unless I'm mistaken. If not, then he was deputy chief. One of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: President Tudjman's view, at least initially, was that you should not be allowed to give testimony at this Tribunal, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know President Tudjman's position. He never spoke to me, and he didn't make his opinion public so I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You talked with Mr. Miljavac -- I'm sorry, it's a hard one for me for some reason. You talked with him for at least two hours, didn't you, after the ICTY summons arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed for up to two hours in his office, when he had summoned me to come, to hand me over the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the course of that conversation, sir, you told Mr. Miljavac that you could come to The Hague to testify and there were any number of things that you could say or any number of interests you could serve, and you were essentially asking for guidances to the effect, What do you want me to say, which interest should I serve?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. You are twisting what I said with regard to the contents of Mr. Miljavac's intervention of what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When President Tudjman ultimately decided that that you would be allowed to testify in the Blaskic case, various steps were taken to prepare answers to the questions that were provided in advance by the Court, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, no steps were taken. On the contrary, not even Minister Miljavac knew what questions I was supposed to answer. They were only interested in how their legal counsel would represent Croatia in that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for example, sir, President Tudjman said you would only be allowed to testify if you testified that the Croatian Army was not in Central Bosnia. If you said that, you would be allowed to testify; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to who Tudjman said that, but he certainly didn't say it to me. The first thing to establish is that I wasn't present at that meeting that you're speaking about, so I don't know what Tudjman said or how he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was a team that was put together that was making special preparations and working with you around that time, prior to your Blaskic testimony, to prepare you for your testimony, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no team worked with me. The team you're mentioning, I don't know based on what they would prepare me to answer the questions that I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit P08912, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the courtroom, this is one of the Presidential transcripts from a meeting on the 13th of April, 1999. It is provided in hard copy, but we're also going to provide it and view it, Your Honours, by way of Sanction, and I believe the first page is on the screen now. But it's P08912, or slide 19. If we can go to -- this is a meeting, you'll see on the cover page, on the 13th of April, 1999, at the offices of President Tudjman, as I've mentioned already. The particular conversation starts on page 31. I'll pause and give people a chance to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Starting on page 31, sir, Mr. Miljavac says: "One more thing, Mr. President, which is coming up. Nobody has paid much attention to it, and I thought I should bring it to your attention. General Petkovic has received a summons to testify. "The President: To testify, where? "In the Blaskic case. In my opinion, this could be a huge trap. He could go there ..." And if we could skip over to page 33, about the middle of the page. The conversation is continuing. We don't have time to go through the entire transcript, word for word: "Now, it is a matter of negotiations with the Tribunal about General Petkovic's status while he is testifying. We have analysed the situation thoroughly and asked for a status conference at which we can reach agreement on clear conditions under which General Petkovic can testify and what he can testify about ..." "The President: And no other questions can be posed there, if that is agreed." To page 34, and the deputy defence minister, Mr. Cosic, comes in: "In this regard, Mr. President, I would like to point out one thing: General Petkovic is a person who spent the most time down there and who was there from the beginning, always at Mr. Boban's side, and covering the whole area of Sarajevo and Central Bosnia during the Croat-Muslim conflict. "Therefore, he is one of the Croatian generals, you will agree, Admiral, you know that, who probably knows the whole story best. There is a high risk that some questions which need not be related to Blaskic at all could be unacceptable for us. General Petkovic knows too much, and taking into account everything he has been through as a soldier, an honourable soldier, and a general, I would not be inclined to put him so lightly in an environment which is still hostile to us." Continuing to the next page, Mr. Rebic comes in. Skipping the first paragraph, Mr. Rebic says: "Furthermore, we have been in direct touch with General Petkovic for three and a half years, for three and a half years we have been working with Petkovic on these things. He has been our associate and helped us to clear up some things while preparing Blaskic's Defence, et cetera. "So he has been in touch with us in continuo, and now he has been undergoing special preparations for several days with a team working on that." I ask you again, sir, when and where did you meet with this team that was preparing you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No team prepared me, Your Honours. I received my summons, I spoke to the minister for up to two hours, and left Zagreb to go to Dubrovnik. This is what they were saying to President Tudjman, who at that moment wasn't even aware of my going -- or my coming here to testify. And Markica Rebic hasn't -- didn't actually prepare me for testifying in the Blaskic case. Rebic took very little part in that. And you know how Blaskic's defence -- to what it came. All these stories they told to President Tudjman are totally unfounded. The Republic of Croatia was able to get a status that gave Mr. Rifkin the right to interrupt me at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they were saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, sir, because our time -- I must continue forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, colleague. I believe -- I'm not quite certain, but I believe that there was -- that something is wrong in the transcript. There is a sentence in line 7 which says: "Rebic took very little part in that." This is not what I understand General Petkovic said. He said Rebic took no part in that, or he said that he didn't have any contact with him. I didn't remember how exactly he said it, but I guess that he should be asked about that, because this is a substantial thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Mr. Rebic didn't have any contact with me, nor did any team have contact with me, as he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The transcript continues, sir -- sir, I'm going to cut you off, and I'm going to have to do that more today. And I'll tell you that in advance, sir, and I apologise for that, but the time simply does not allow either you or I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think this is not fair --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me -- excuse me, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Don't interrupt me. Excuse me, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The witness should be given an opportunity to correct the transcript, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He just did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- the counsel is interrupting witness in half of the sentence when he's doing exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I allowed the witness very specifically to answer the part where he said Mr. Rebic did not, in his view, according to him, did not play a part in that, and I allowed him to give that answer. And then he's going on about other matters, and I don't have the time. If the Chamber wants to give me more time, I'm happy to take it, but I cannot allow Mr. Petkovic to go on and on about everything that he'd like to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... to trap me, Prosecutor, and I can't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're on your feet because -- the Defence counsel are on their feet because you answered in your language. Since the Defence counsel know both languages, English and B/C/S, they are saying, Be careful, there is a problem on the transcript. That is why you're on your feet, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honours. I just wanted to make my -- make the objection of Mr. Kovacic more specific. Page 12, line 7, I believe, Mr. Kovacic said, the continuation of the answer about Markica Rebic was that Rebic was not involved in the preparation of the Defence of General Blaskic, either, and that the Prosecution at this trial knows best how things ended up with Rebic and Blaskic. That's what the general said, and I believe that it is in everybody's interest that we be accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said, that he didn't take part in Blaskic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly what I allowed the witness to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we continue over to page 36, please, in the transcript, Mr. Tudjman comes back in: "This should be done in advance. Therefore, the general can go and can answer only these questions in writing." And it might be of some interest, but we won't take time to read it all, but Mr. Gotovina apparently was opposed to your coming to The Hague, Mr. Petkovic. And we'll continue over on to page 38. On page 38, Mr. Domazet says, about the middle of the page: "So, this is clear. If it is decided that General Petkovic should go, he will be in an even more difficult situation than I was," I think that should say, "that is clear. The questions and answers must be defined exactly and precisely. Nothing beyond that." Now, Mr. Domazet makes it very clear here the questions and answers must be defined exactly and precisely. I put it to you, sir, that that's exactly what happened. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that's not what happened. The Republic of Croatia is in no position to prepare the Tribunal's questions and answers so Petkovic can go back to them and read them back and forth. I think this is ridiculous, the very idea that Croatia should be preparing the Q and A and then Petkovic would be appearing in court and start off saying, Your Honours, this is a question by the Republic of Croatia, and then this is the answer. Come on. Have you ever seen evidence being given like that before this Tribunal? Is that your idea of how things work here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it wasn't apparently a joke to these men. I'm not making this up. I'm reading to you from the official record of the meeting. That's what they thought should happen. These aren't Ken Scott's words. And, yes, it could happen -- no, of course you wouldn't be expected to say, Well, I was told by the Tudjman group to say this, but you could come to the Tribunal and say exactly what you were told to say, couldn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 40 --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Top of page 40, Mr. Miljavac says: "I talked to him for two hours --"

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "I talked to him for two hours when the summons arrived --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let Mr. Scott ask his questions. You are to answer them. Please continue, because I will have a question after you. Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "I talked to him for two hours when the summons arrived, and he said the following:" Now, he says these are your words, not his, sir: "You know that I can go and testify in Blaskic's favour or in the favour of the Republic of Croatia. You must decide:"

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "You must decide --" stop interrupting me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask the Chamber to instruct the witness to stop interrupting my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, please listen to the Prosecutor first, because he's reading out what Mr. Miljavac said. So please listen carefully. He's going to put a question to you and then you can answer and give your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "You know that I can go and testify in Blaskic's favour or in the favour of the Republic of Croatia. You must decide. I asked him what he meant. Just that, he said, because I know everything. It is a matter of deciding what to build our defence on. He said, it is very risky for me to go." And that's the conversation that you told us about a few minutes ago, that you said when you meet with Mr. Miljavac about the summons, and you met with him for approximately two hours, which is exactly what he says here, that's the conversation you had with him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this has nothing to do with what I actually talked to Mr. Miljavac about. As I've already told the Trial Chamber, I met Miljavac, and he was in charge of this conversation, saying that the Republic of Croatia made sure it had a legal representative, and should anyone ask any questions at all about the Republic of Croatia, this legal representative would have the right to stop it. After about an hour and a half of talking to him, I asked Mr. Miljavac, Mr. Miljavac, tell me, please, am I on my way to give evidence in the Blaskic case or is this a case against the Republic of Croatia? The question simply suggested itself. He didn't ask me how I was feeling, what sort of evidence I would be giving. He kept telling me, We have a legal representative who'll be doing this and doing that, and you will hardly get a chance to answer. I didn't know what questions I would be asked, I didn't know what answers I would be giving. And the questions about the Tribunal -- the questions that I got at the Tribunal have nothing whatsoever to do with the Republic of Croatia. It's a matter of public record. If you want to, you can go back to the transcript on that trial and read it for yourself. It is another matter [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Petkovic, you want to be heard and understood, and that needs interpretation. You are simply speaking too fast. The interpreters have difficulties, and then you don't come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you suggesting that Mr. Miljavac, the minister of defence -- this is no small person. This is the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, who at least at the time thinks he's having an important private meeting with other senior officials of the Government of Croatia, including President Tudjman, and are you suggesting he just made these words up; that he gave this account of what you told him in a conversation and he just made this up in telling the other people in the meeting, including President Tudjman, what you had told him in your meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said to Miljavac at the meeting does not tally with what it says here. I'll stand by this for as long as you keep asking questions about it. Secondly, the gentleman could have invited me to that meeting and not say, Petkovic is off to Dubrovnik. And they went to see President Tudjman -- to a particular meeting, and suddenly it crossed the minister's mind to say, Mr. President, you know there's a letter saying that Petkovic should go and give evidence, and the president had no idea about that, he had no idea that a letter had arrived. And then the whole story began. Each of those involved there would give their own version. Meanwhile, Petkovic was 600 kilometres away, on his way to Dubrovnik. That is what I'm trying to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: President Tudjman says: "At this moment, I'm in favour of a decision banning Croatian generals from going to The Hague, either as witnesses or as accused persons." Continuing on to page 41, Tudjman says again: "If you will, he can go and testify about whether there were regular Croatian units in the Lasva Valley, if his answer to that is, No, he can go, but nothing else." And that's part of the instructions you were given, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it isn't. I was given no instructions. No one else was, either. Tudjman cannot impose questions on a Trial Chamber. Obviously, President Tudjman had no idea, either, how business was conducted before this Tribunal. He would have been in no position to set any conditions for the Trial Chamber. Nevertheless, President Tudjman and the Croatian government managed to ensure the services of a legal representative. It was the first time ever in that trial that Croatia enlisted the assistance of a legal representative. I don't know how they were granted the power to do that by this Tribunal, but this legal representative had the right to stop me at any point throughout my evidence. Croatia did not need Petkovic. Croatia got itself a legal representative, who turned up, appeared there, and stepped in twice, maybe as many as three times, when an extension of my evidence was required spilling over into the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 42, sir, it says Ante Gotovina says: "Our soldiers fought in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. I was the commander of the Livno Municipal Staff of the HVO. Therefore, this cannot be hidden ..." This can't be hidden, this can't be kept from the Tribunal. Skipping to the next paragraph: "Therefore, they are taking him to The Hague because they have a plan, while Blaskic's Defence is defending only Blaskic, not the interests of the Republic of Croatia." "If Blaskic is trying to save himself and get out as soon as possible, good for him, but we must keep in mind that there are definitely attempts to involve the supreme leadership of the Republic of Croatia. If we give them every time ..." Tudjman: "You in The Hague group, OA Haag, you in The Hague group, go ahead and deal with it. I do not have a definite position. I am inclined to say that no Croatian general should go there, neither as a witness or as an accused person." And then skipping over -- skip over to page 44, toward the end of that page. Mr. Rebic is talking again. Mr. Rebic then -- they go further, even, sir. Actually, pardon me. Rebic, at the beginning of that page 44, Mr. Rebic says: "There are no signs Nobilo did not shift any blame to the Croatian state so far, not to the state. To some parallel structures down there, yes ..." And the Croatian Defence Minister says: "Markica, six of one, half a dozen of the other, you know." The people in that meeting had no trouble understanding that to talk about Croatia, on the one hand, and to talk about Herceg-Bosna, on the other, was six of one, half a dozen of the other. They knew they were one and the same thing, didn't they ?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would be objecting -- I will be objecting at this point in time. I'm told that there's a translation problem, but now he's -- the general is being asked to give an opinion as to what others thought. He can talk about what he thought, but at this point in time, I think for the general to be giving an opinion as to what they thought or what this particular individual thought about Croatia and Herceg-Bosna is improper. It not only calls for speculation, but it's asking him to divine what exactly they meant at that meeting, at which he was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I'll come back to another topic, Your Honours. I'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on, Mr. Rebic, toward the bottom of the page, says: "... how Blaskic defines the command system is intended to remove the blame from himself, but it is not true. It is a material falsehood." Continuing over to the top of page 45: "There can be a collision there. If General Petkovic goes there and speaks the truth, they will have to pull down part of Blaskic's position, because Blaskic quite unsuccessfully went into that double subordination ..." And the president says: "... Unnecessarily" -- my apologies, "quite unnecessarily went into that double subordination ..." The president: "But if there is a collision between Petkovic and Blaskic, things get more complicated. Thank you, gentlemen. Goodbye." Sir, you said yesterday afternoon, and you said again today, the Croatian government displayed no interest whatsoever in the content of your evidence, it was never agreed with anyone, no one controlled your testimony, no one influenced you. And, sir, I put it -- it become very clear from this meeting that the Croatian government, at least these people around Tudjman, were extremely concerned about the content of the testimony that you would give if you came to The Hague, and you knew that, sir. You knew these people. One was your minister. You'd met with Tudjman before. You were a senior leader of Herceg-Bosna, as we've talked about yesterday. You knew what these concerns were. And when they said you knew too much, you knew that to be exactly the case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They held this talk without me. Anyone talking in my absence -- well, what they're talking has nothing to do with it. This is their story. What bearing does this story have on this trial or any other trial before this Tribunal? None at all. They simply are entirely unaware of how things work, in a procedural sense. They were talking to each other, and that concerns no one else. It would have been logical, after this meeting, for someone to call me up, Petkovic, come over, let's have a talk, but there was nothing there. All you have is what they said on that day, the exchanges that went on, and that's all you've got. The day I was supposed to testify, there was no one there. The government representative took me to the UNPROFOR base, left me there, and I remained there with a secretary and a technician from the Tribunal. There was no one to ask me any questions that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because Mr. Rifkin [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what they said at that meeting, and you know full well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because Mr. Rifkin and Mr. Udiljak were sitting in the courtroom here, protecting the interests of the Government of Croatia, and you knew that. You just told us, sir. But don't pretend that they weren't involved. They were sitting in this courtroom, deciding on what questions you could answer and which ones you couldn't -- wouldn't be allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Jorda was the Presiding Judge, and he was listening and dealing with them. And they would tell him, Well, you know, he can answer this question, he can't answer some other questions, weren't they? That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's the way it always is. We had an American ambassador, and, as I recall, we had a couple of American -- young, bright American lawyers working for the State Department here. We had from other governments, and I don't need to mention them. They all brought their lawyers. Holbrooke, when he claimed that he was going to come here, he want to get his marching orders from Washington, and they were going to work out the modalities as to what he would be willing or able to talk about. If you asked the American government for any information, they neither confirm nor deny that they have it, because of national security interests. Even when it isn't a national security interest, that's the way it is. A government is entitled to have their representative when an ambassador, or former ambassador, or somebody in an official capacity is giving testimony, so there's no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't suggest that there was or that this was a unique situation, but what I was responding to was Mr. Petkovic's -- some attempts to suggest that he was left by himself, fending for himself at an UNPROFOR base in Zagreb, and that wasn't the case at all. And that was my point. Of course, I'm fully aware of what Mr. Karnavas has said, but the Chamber does know -- the Chamber does know, by the transcript it has just read, the fuller picture of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir -- and that's the way it was. And, in fact, following this meeting it was Mr. Miljavac who successfully limited your appearance, at least initially, to one day only, and that was specifically for the purpose of limiting the amount of questions that could be put to you and how much information might be gathered from you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to do with that. As I've told the Chamber already, the Republic of Croatia was in charge of the entire procedure. I was in Dubrovnik at the time. I was informed at one point in time under what conditions I would be giving evidence. As soon as I learned of that, I was to fill a form and send it off to the Trial Chamber, as I did. The Chamber's reply was a positive one, so I came and testified. No one can prepare a Q and A session for something to happen before this Tribunal and tell a person what responses to provide. Don't say that, because it didn't work like that. As to what the Croatian government did, well, it's their problem, not mine. I realised how things worked. At one point in time, I sat down, I said that I was off to The Hague myself, on my own, without the assistance of the Croatian government, and that I would be testifying on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you last speak or have any involvement with Mr. Udiljak, this Croatian intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Udiljak was a member of the Council for Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal, which at the time was headed by Croatia's prime minister at the time and some ministers. He was a member of that body, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That really wasn't my question. You're using my time. When was the last time you had contact with -- answer my question, sir. When was the last time you had contact with Mr. Udiljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specify the time. While this whole procedure was in progress, prior to my testimony and after my testimony, Mr. Udiljak would ask whether I was reading the papers and what they said about how people were testifying, and that was the extent of Mr. Udiljak's questions to me. And I said, Yes, I'm following the media. And what do you think, he said. I said, It's not my problem, is it? Let each man testify --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. You're not answering my question and you know it. I said when is the last time you had contact with Mr. Udiljak. It has nothing to do with his questions about whether you're reading the newspapers in 1999. When was the last time? Prior to today, prior to right now, when was the last time you had contact with Mr. Udiljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the last time prior to this day. How could I possibly remember when I was in touch with Mr. Udiljak, who retired five or six years ago, perhaps more? He's now retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Has Mr. Udiljak been involved in the preparation of this case or providing assistance in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not to me. He provided no assistance to me and was no part of my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question isn't limited to you, sir. Has he been providing assistance in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me, not that I'm aware of. I'm not sure if my Defence team can contribute whether they were perhaps in touch with Mr. Udiljak. I think he was in contact with an altogether different Defence team, and I don't think he could possibly have been in contact with two different teams at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I told you once, sir, my question wasn't limited to your Defence. So if Mr. Udiljak has been involved in this case, tell us about his involvement.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know, he was helping General Praljak's Defence. I'm not sure about the extent, though. Mr. Udiljak was at no point in time in touch with the Petkovic Defence, that is, my Defence, or, indeed, offer or give any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this was the same Mr. Udiljak who was coming to this Tribunal at a time when the Croatian government was telling this Tribunal it didn't have the HVO archive, when, in fact, it was sitting in the basement of the Croatian Intelligence Service, wasn't it? HIS, H-I-S.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Udiljak told you at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, what he told me. It was the same, and you knew it, sir. You've been close to these events. Mr. Rebic said, We've been working with Mr. Petkovic for three and a half years, and you knew what was going on, you knew the lay of the land. And you followed these matters close enough to know that for a long time, the Tudjman government was denying it had the documents, was coming before this Tribunal, was appearing before Judge Jorda and others, and saying, We don't have any documents. But they did, and they were sitting in the basement of the Intelligence Service. And they knew that, and you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that, Your Honours. I wasn't living in Zagreb at the time. I wasn't [Realtime transcript read in error "was"] living with them there. I wasn't meeting those people at the time, nor, indeed, was that any of my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unless the Court has any --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction. Line 16: [In English] "I was living with them there." [Interpretation] Whereas, the General clearly said he wasn't. General, is that right? What exactly did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I wasn't living with them there. I was at Croatia's far end, 600 kilometres further south, in Dubrovnik, whereas they were in Zagreb at the time. Therefore, I didn't belong to the circle of people doing intelligence work or anything like that. What they did was their own worry. I had no part in that, nor, indeed, was I interested. I only know that I walked away from Herceg-Bosna at one point and the documents remained there, the same place where I left them. I'm not sure for how long, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on. And if the Judges have questions on this topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General Petkovic, given the topic which is an important one, and do you agree with me on that point, I have a few questions for you. First of all, the Prosecutor's shown you a document. Were you aware of it? Had you read it before you started testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I was not aware of it. I received my summons, and then no one approached me again before the Blaskic trial began.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you please just specify which evidence you mean? Today's evidence or the one that occurred 10 years ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, General Petkovic, I wasn't precise enough. I'm speaking about the document that the Prosecutor showed you, this Presidential transcript, and now you're testifying here now before us. I'm not talking about the Blaskic case 10 years ago. When you started, were you aware of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure how long after exactly, but the magazine called "Nacional" published some of this. Other than that, I've not seen the document nor did anyone inform me of what occurred. "Nacional" wrote about this document. I'm not sure at what point in time exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please specify? Your Honour Judge Antonetti asked about the transcript, whether you knew about the transcript before you took the witness stand here. Did you read this transcript during this trial? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not now. The transcript, you mean? I read it because it was part of my material. I thought you were asking whether someone informed me of it. No, no, I did that at my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, did you expect the Prosecutor to ask the question he's just asked you or are you totally taken by surprise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I expected with a degree of certainty that they would be asking questions on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move to the substance - I'll get there - but I see that Judge Trechsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to clarify a point, Mr. Petkovic. In the transcript here, on page 29, line 9, I read: "The transcript, you mean?" You speaking, "I read it because it was part of my material." Are you referring to the transcript that was put to you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received parts of this transcript as part of our materials. I believe some of these were published in book form in Croatia at one point, but we received them as part of our batch of documents for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not want any explanation. I just wanted to be sure that there was no mistake in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, before we move to the substance of the document, and you'll see why this is important soon, when you were in Croatia, when you learned that you were supposed to testify, you were called to testify by the Blaskic Trial Chamber, regardless of the part of the Croatian Defence Ministry, you, personally, did you go and see a lawyer in order to explain what the situation was about, that you'd been summoned, and ask that lawyer what he thought of it, or did you not see any lawyer and did you just have meetings with your ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not have a lawyer, myself. I prepared when I received the summons, and then I reported to Zagreb to take delivery of the Trial Chamber's summons. I did not have any legal representative or counsel, nor, indeed, was I minded to take one on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw the document, as I did, and you listened to the Prosecutor as he was reading out some excerpts. There are two points in this document that are clearly emphasised, and you said so yourself regarding the first part. General [as interpreted] Tudjman discovered that the Tribunal sought to hear you, because he says, Where? So obviously he discovered this. I'm talking about him, President Tudjman. I don't know about the others, but he seems to discover the problem. Secondly, and this is said by President Tudjman in person, he said that there's a so-called Hague group. Now, when you received the summons, did you know of the existence of a so-called Hague group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I only knew that there was an office of the Cabinet of the Republic of Croatia, an office for the co-operation with the ICTY. And as far as I know, the vice-prime minister was the head of that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were not to -- if I didn't put to you this question, I wouldn't be doing my job. You are a professional in the military, and I'm a professional in legal matters. I must put to you the following question, which has to do with the substance of the document: On looking at this document, we see that a number of people take the floor as regards the question of people taking the stand and the accused, because Gotovina, who is well known, takes part in the discussion. This is what the document states. On reading the document, we can see that President Tudjman hesitates. First of all, he doesn't want the General to testify, but, on the other hand, those people attending the meeting are saying that it's difficult not to go. And then there's General Gotovina, who, for technical reasons, seems to be totally hostile. This is what the document states. In this document, you can also see that Mr. Rebic says that there is a preparation which is being done with you. Any reasonable trier of fact has only two assumptions to consider. Either Mr. Rebic is talking nonsense to the president, which is quite possible, either for personal reasons or to put himself forward, I don't know, but that could be an assumption. The second one is that there was this preparation. To try and understand, when I listened to the Prosecutor and your answers, I looked at page 22.617. As you know, General Petkovic, I've been preparing for your testimony for the last two years, and I had some pages at the ready, and these are public pages or pages heard in open session, since everything is public. 22.617, I apologise to the English speakers, I shall read out the page. Judge Shahabuddeen, whom you know, retired after having worked a number of years in this Tribunal. He did draft a number of dissenting opinions, so he's quite well known in the Tribunal. This is the question he put to you. Listen carefully: "General, another issue, if you'll allow me." Mr. Shahabuddeen was an extremely well-behaved gentleman and asked you whether he would be allowed to put this question to you: "When you were head of the Main Staff, were you paid by the HVO authorities or by the Croatian authorities?" So he's doing his job, he's putting to you a question of a technical nature. Your answer, listen carefully. I shall read it very slowly, because I believe it's important: "Your Honour, in the course of my preparation, I was never faced with such a question. The representative of the Republic of Croatia is present in the courtroom. If he wishes to answer, he may do so. As far as I'm concerned, as well as all the other witnesses, we have received instructions to only answer the questions that have been given to us beforehand, but the representative of the Republic of Croatia may take the floor. If he instructs me to, I shall then answer." Mr. Shahabuddeen then says this: "General, my position is that I would like to avoid embarrassing the representative of the Republic of Croatia. I shall withdraw my question." And President Jorda, quoted by Mr. Scott, the Judge then withdrew his question: "Thank you." So two things follow from your answers. A, you say, In the course of my preparation. When you say, In the course of my preparation, this means that you accept the idea that you were preparing beforehand. B, you said, We received instructions, which means that the Ministry of Defence did monitor your answers. Do you remember your answers? Do you say that you are -- or that you testified freely and that you weren't prepped in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the very question I've wanted to answer. When I started answering a short while ago, there was a misunderstanding between me and the President of the Trial Chamber, and I said, Well, then I -- there's a misunderstanding between you and I with regard to the questions I received to prepare. Do you wish me to start this way or move on to a specific question? And the President said, Let's move on to specific questions, but he allowed me an introduction. These questions I mentioned were the questions I received from the Trial Chamber and based on which I prepared. And I replied that in my preparation and in my questions, there was nothing concerning matters contained in the question asked by the Judge to me. So I thought the questions that I had received from the President of the Trial Chamber were the ones to which he wishes to hear answers, and I prepared based on these questions. And that is why I said, Your Honour, I didn't deal with such questions during my preparation because such questions weren't given to me by the Trial Chamber, and we can go back to the list of questions, and you will see that -- what they were. And then I continued to say to the President of the Trial Chamber that I had been informed that the legal counsel of the Republic of Croatia is the one to decide whether I will answer any questions concerning the Republic of Croatia. And, of course, I obeyed because that was the agreement between Croatia and this Tribunal. I had no role in that. So when I refer to questions, I mean the questions that I received from the Trial Chamber. I got some questions, I gave them a thought, sketched out my answers to them, and hence I said that I didn't prepare to answer this question because it wasn't one of those that were given to me. I had been told by the Republic of Croatia, We managed to get the right to be represented by a lawyer, and that there was an agreement giving that lawyer the right to interrupt me. In other words, he would be the one to listen to the questions and say, Yes, the General can answer. And that was what I said in the first few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I note that under oath you are saying that there was no preparation. You prepared your testimony in the Blaskic trial all on your own, based on the questions which the Trial Chamber had forwarded to you, and nobody intervened. This is what you've said. I have noted this. One last question. In the document, we have seen -- perhaps you will be able to shed some light on this, because I haven't quite understood what General Gotovina's role was here. He is worried about Blaskic and you. He is concerned about the twofold subordination. I'm not quite sure what this means. Could you shed some light on this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that General Gotovina at that time had a position in the inspectorate of the Croatian Army. Whether or not he was chief inspector, I'm not sure. And that was a group of generals who constantly went to see President Tudjman, from General Gotovina, Cosic, Minister Miljavac, Mr. Domazet, and I don't know who else joined them. So it was a group that went to see the president every once in a while. They discussed with him. What they discussed was never made public. Why General Gotovina said what he said and what he had in mind, I simply don't know, because in the Blaskic case, I know that the Blaskic case has a substantial bearing on me. There was no way I could get away from the possibility that an indictment could be issued against me tomorrow. I was fully aware that, based on the questions I had received, I had to speak my mind and the truth during that testimony, and nothing else but that. I never burdened myself with questions apart from those that I had received. Of course, I don't know what you are about to ask me now or at any other time. Nobody can know in that in advance. On the other hand, Your Honours, President Tudjman and everybody else could have said whatever they wanted, but they knew that I had to come here to testify, irrespective of what they said, whether they would allow it or not. They knew that, and I knew that, too, because I had followed how things worked here. So all this time they spent at the president's office was wasted. They even received a summons without informing President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I would like to discuss this twofold subordination. I'd like to remain technical in my question, because this could be understood two ways. There is a chain of command which is a traditional chain of command; Boban, you, Blaskic. That would be the standard form of subordination. Do you agree with me? But there could also be, and that might be another way of seeing things when Gotovina mentions this dual subordination, there could be the other side that could be Blaskic and Boban, in direct line, and you are on the side-line. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He obviously thought that apart from what I call the normal line, possibly another line of commanding may have been introduced. Gotovina knows, because he was at high positions in the Croatian Army, too, what the line of -- the chain of command was, so he may have wondered whether a parallel chain of command had come into being. He probably meant some other chain of command apart from the regular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As this meeting took place in Zagreb between high-ranking Croatians, could there not be a connection with the chain of command that would be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, right up to Zagreb? Is that a possibility? Is this something which one could consider or was it a crazy idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you can't even make up in your mind such a chain directly from Central Bosnia to Zagreb. I can't even imagine such a chain of command that would go directly from Vitez to Zagreb. It's impossible for me even to envisage it or assume that it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I shall put my last question to you, which follows from your answer. I understand full well that you are telling us that there's only one chain of command, which is the internal Bosnia and Herzegovina chain of command. If that is the case, why do they all seem so worried? Why is Tudjman worried? Why is the minister of defence worried? Why is Gotovina worried? Why is Rebic worried? Why are they worried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that none of them really followed the Blaskic trial. Blaskic selected his own team that followed it. Everybody else was -- wasn't really involved. Blaskic had been extradited, and nobody else seems to have thought that they had anything more to do with that. I was one of the witnesses at a high level, and everybody else was at a lower level inside the Central Bosnia OZ, so I was one of the most highest-ranking witnesses, and I had returned to the Croatian Army, so I was actually a Croatian official. And there was some confusion about the transcript, so contact had been set up with the Tribunal as to what should happen next. This was the first instance when there was a lawyer representing Croatia. I don't think that this was repeated after my testimony, either. So the technical conditions were agreed upon by them, not by me, and I informed the Trial Chamber, who simply accepted. I don't know why. They could have refused. But the President of the Trial Chamber accepted the conditions, and that's how I came to The Hague to testify. And the second time around, as soon as I received the summons, I drafted a letter, myself, to the Trial Chamber, saying that I would come to The Hague. I never contacted anybody in Zagreb about that. And that's how it went, because I had decided to -- to decide myself about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I have a small question which goes back to the scene where Judge Shahabuddeen asked you, Who paid for your salary? And then you refused answering, if I understood you correctly, giving two reasons. First, you were not prepared for this question, and, second, it was not one of the questions you were expressly allowed to answer. Now, the second point has been argued. I will not refer to that. But the first point I find difficult to understand. In what way could the answer to that question need preparation? Did you not know who had paid for your salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew who was paying out my salary, but I had already noticed that the lawyer was rising, asking for the floor, when that question was asked. I was going to say that this wasn't one of the questions that I had received from the Trial Chamber, and I referred them to the lawyer who had already stood up to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So, in fact, lack of preparation was not an argument that you raised. That makes sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll start with the last point just made, touched on by both Judge Trechsel and Judge Antonetti. Sir, that wasn't the last time the salary question was put to you. And as was just said by the Judges, you certainly didn't need any preparation. You knew how you were being paid and where it was coming from. When you came back and testified in the Kordic case, you were again accompanied by representatives of the Croatian government, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were only Croatian Embassy staff, no lawyer or anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. That wasn't my question and you're wasting time, to be honest, General. My question was: You were represented by a representative of the Croatian government? And the answer is, Yes. The answer is clearly, Yes. We have the appearances on the record. They stood up in court, introduced themselves as representing the Croatian government, so there's no mystery about that, sir. And on that occasion, sir, you were also asked about who would pay your salary --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have an objection now, because the situation is very different. If representatives of the embassy are present here to represent the Croatian government, that's one thing, and another thing if they are present as representatives of General Petkovic before the Tribunal. There's no reason for us to confuse these two situations, and there is no reason why Mr. Scott should put forward false statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and these people had no authority. They were sitting in a corner back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. And my position, I believe, unless I'm not mistaken, and if I am, I apologise, but I thought I was clear. I said to you, sir, you were attended on that occasion again by representatives of the Croatian government, and you were. And that's -- and it's just purely that simple, isn't it? I don't care if they came from the embassy, I don't care if they came from Zagreb, I don't care if they came from Split. You were attended by representatives of the Croatian government, representing the interests of Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have met these people in the courtroom. I didn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer is, Yes, sir? Sir, the answer is, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is, Yes. They were from the embassy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were asked again about your salary, seven or eight times, at least, in the transcript. You wouldn't answer the question. The question was quite clear. You're an intelligent man. You knew the question would be asked. It was put to you by Mr. Nice, it was put to you by several of the Judges, and it was only about the eighth or ninth time, when you were pressed by Judge Robinson, that you finally, finally, said, Well, I was paid approximately half my salary by Herceg-Bosna and the other half or 60 per cent by Croatia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not five or six times, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, if we can look -- the Judges have your transcript from Kordic, and they all follow it, and if we need to, I'll put out the pages later. But you were repeatedly asked the question, you repeatedly evaded, you repeatedly refused to answer the question, and it was only when Judge Robinson continued to press you that you finally gave the answer that, as Judge Trechsel said a moment ago, you'd needed no preparation for. You finally were pressed to give the answer you didn't want to give, and that was 50 to 60 per cent of your salary was being paid by Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but I also had to think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why didn't you want to tell the Court that, sir? Why did you take so long? Why, in the Blaskic case, could you not answer the question? Why, in the Kordic case, were you asked five, six, seven times? Why didn't you want the Court to have that information?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking about my payment transactions, because money had been paid to my savings account and that doesn't allow you to see who paid in money. And when it came to Herceg-Bosna, I was promised that money would be taken care of. And when somebody pays onto a savings account, you had to remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You knew full well, because when you couldn't avoid it anymore, you gave the answer, you gave the answer, and you knew it all the time. It didn't just spring into your mind on the seventh or eighth time. You knew the answer, and you only gave it when you really had no other choice, sir, I put it to you, and you knew that, and those were part of the instructions that you had received from the very beginning, When you go down there, sir -- when you go up there, I suppose, When you go to The Hague, don't talk about your connection to Croatia when you were in the HVO, don't talk about the HVO's relation to the Croatian Army, don't talk about those connections. And you followed your instructions, and you refused to talk about it until you were finally -- on the second court appearance in the second case, pressed by Judge Robinson, you finally gave up that information, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was thinking, trying to remember whether I could reconstruct the payments affected onto my account and where that payment had come from, because once I had arrived to Herceg-Bosna I wanted to resolve the financial matters. And I was promised that there would be no problem about that -- with that and that I would be entitled to some additional benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have your position, sir. We have your position. You said a few moments ago, in response to Judge -- the President's question, about whether there was concern about, in fact -- part of the concern being whether the chain of command could be traced back to Zagreb, and you were -- I'm not sure why, but you were so quickly dismissive of that, as if it was -- and you said, and I have it marked at page 37 of today's transcript, line 8: "No, you can't make up in your own mind such a chain directly from Central Bosnia to Zagreb, I can't even imagine such a chain of command." Well, sir, I can imagine a chain of command. It goes from Blaskic, to you, to Boban, to Susak, and Bobetko to Tudjman. I can imagine it real easily, and I don't know why you find that so difficult. And that's exactly what Zagreb, and what Tudjman, and the people sitting in his office on the 13th of April, 1999, that's what they were so concerned about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, they say so, sir. They say so. At page 42 of the transcript, P08912, Gotovina talking, second half of the page, I read this before, but apparently it didn't sink in: "Therefore, they are taking him to The Hague because they have a plan, while Blaskic's Defence is defending only Blaskic, not the interests of the Republic of Croatia. We should see it that way for the time being. If Blaskic is trying to save himself and get out as soon as possible, good for him, but we must keep in mind that there are definitely attempts to involve the supreme leadership of the Republic of Croatia. If we give them every time," and I think what he's saying, "If we give in every time ..." And then Tudjman jumps in: "Nothing to imagine, sir." Mr. Gotovina put it there in black and white, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask one thing, please. Let's try to be as specific as we can when we phrase our questions, and let us not draw the conclusion that Gotovina said something he did not, in fact, say. All of us here are well familiar with the Blaskic case. We know his theory on the parallel chain of command and what it leads to. There is no need at all to refer to anything that wasn't actually said in the Blaskic trial or in the present trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I quoted the transcript, Your Honours, word for word. I didn't make up anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it was widely regarded -- in fact, it was widely regarded, after you returned to Zagreb -- excuse me, after you finished your testimony in the Blaskic case, and I should say -- maybe it hasn't been clear and maybe it may have been a point of some confusion. You gave your testimony by videolink. You were in Croatia, and the people here were in the courtroom, and Croatia's representatives, Mr. Rifkin and Mr. Udiljak, were sitting in court. You were connected by videolink, correct, just so that's clear?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you finished your testimony, sir, and we all know -- everyone in this room or many of us knows that there's quite an active -- I suppose in most countries, active media, you had "Nacional," you had "Globus," you had all the local newspapers, and it was quite extensive coverage, albeit it was supposed to be in closed session, but there was quite extensive coverage to the effect that you had come here and committed perjury. That's what the newspapers said. You had come here to protect the interests of Croatia, and if that meant possibly doing damages to Mr. Blaskic's case, so be it, but your marching orders had been to come to The Hague, protect the interests of Croatia and the Tudjman government, and that's what you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. The newspapers said what they said. You should perhaps ask the newspapers how they know what I testified to. Since I testified in closed session, there was no way for the media to get wind of it. This was something that was down to Mr. Nobilo, the Defence counsel in that case, and those newspapers that favoured him such as "Nacional" and other sources like that. There is no way these newspapers could possibly get wind of something that goes on in closed session. Yet, they arrived at the conclusion that I gave evidence here. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How about a copy of your transcript, your closed-session transcript that would have been leaked to the media, because that happened repeatedly, didn't it? In fact, even Mr. Mesic's testimony, when Mr. Mesic came and gave closed-session testimony, it very quickly found its way on the papers in Zagreb, didn't it? Didn't it, sir, statement? You know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm really not sure whether Mr. Scott is perhaps insinuating that General Petkovic was the person who handed over the transcripts to the media, particularly those criticising him, including the transcript of Mr. Mesic's evidence. I really have no idea what these insinuations are supposed to achieve. General Petkovic knew the transcript that bears the date of the 17th of January, 2008. That's when it became an exhibit. He knows every single word in this case. He's prepared to clarify and explain any question at all. I would ask the Chamber, however, to please caution Mr. Scott to run his examination in a fair manner, to not dispute facts that are beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I did not have the impression that he was -- Mr. Scott was insinuating that Mr. Petkovic would have leaked the transcripts. I don't know whether my colleagues don't agree or not. They would say so if they are. He just said that the media wrote or reported on what was said in closed session, but he didn't say it came from a certain person. Never did he say such a thing. Well, that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing for me. Let me address a point that was discussed twice. On one occasion, I put the question, myself, about the salary. You answered on page 39, line 1 of the transcript. Since I'm going to quote the transcript, I'm going to return to English: [In English] Your answer was: "I knew who was paying out my salary." And some minutes later, asked the same question by Mr. Scott and asked for explanation why you took so long to give an answer on this, you suddenly came up with all sorts of difficulties and things that you did not know, and that was later than the Blaskic trial. Can you explain this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Actually, before this explanation, I would only like to say that, as it was indicated already by our President, Judge Antonetti, I have never felt that Mr. Scott's question was in a way insinuating that those information was leaked out by Mr. Petkovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'll answer Judge Trechsel's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, please. You must, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. That's why I was asking permission. I was receiving my salary through a bank called Privedna Banka. I would receive this at my home address, and not in Herzegovina, where I was staying at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not interested in that at all. I'm only interested in the fact that to my question, you simply answered, I knew who was paying out my salary, and when Mr. Scott asked you, Didn't you know who paid your salary, you said, In fact, it was difficult to find out. I had to think, and I -- only after being asked several times did it occur to me how it was. And I find it difficult not to find a discrepancy between the first answer and the second answer, and it's only this that I ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because the questions are phrased differently and then I provide different answers. That's why. I paused for a while there and tried to think back. I had agreed that payments would be made from Grude, which is where I was at the time, and then I paused to think whether I could form an idea in my head as to whether the money actually arrived from Grude or from Croatia's Defence Ministry, which had been the case up until then. Having thought about it, I realised that -- please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Petkovic, you are not answering my question, but I will not insist. I think it's time for the break, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before the break, if I may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't interrupt me just like that, for all sorts of reasons. I don't think it makes any sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the General should be allowed to complete his answer. This is far from being the first time that Judge Trechsel interrupts the General, expresses his dissatisfaction at the answer, and says all sorts of things --
