utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which counsel proceeds to quote in English, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [In English] I will leave the Prosecution to clear up the matter. [Interpretation] I really think that is entirely unfair, and the General should be allowed to provide any answers that he thinks he should. You can take his answer or leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Judge Trechsel is going to answer, but let me say this: You are now saying that my fellow Judge interrupted the witness because he was not satisfied. How can you say this? The Judge asked a question, and he expects an answer. Apparently, there's a problem in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. This was a misinterpretation. I'll try to say slowly what I just said. I said I believe this is not the first time that Judge Trechsel interrupts an answer by the General and expresses his dissatisfaction at the answer. Nevertheless, he always says he would leave it to the OTP to clarify matters and take them as far as necessary. I believe the witness should be allowed to complete his answers, to complete what he's trying to say. It is down to the Judge to evaluate his answer as a valid one or not. It never even crossed my mind to say that the Judge was interrupting because he was unhappy, and I didn't say that, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Alaburic, in a way, I was unhappy, because I heard a story where I wanted an explanation on a very narrow point. You seem to introduce new rules here. We have always, and rightly so -- everyone in the courtroom, I think, insisted that when a question is asked, the witness cannot say what he wants to say, but he has to answer the specific question. And if he goes astray and speaks of something which the person who has put the question does not recognise as leading to an answer to the question, it is his duty, in order to save time, to interrupt the witness and try to lead him back to the track on which he has been set by the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may. Something different, because I'm not going to get into this discussion. Rightly or wrongly, my opinion doesn't matter. But what I am concerned is the line of questioning by the Prosecution, and I agree, he was not insinuating that it was General Petkovic who was leaking the material, so that was my understanding as well, but it would appear that the government, or through its representatives, may be doing all these harmful things. The problem is the government is not on trial. The Croatian government doesn't have a representative here to defend Croatia. And how do I now, representing Dr. Prlic, challenge this line of questioning at this stage, if you are to then accept the Prosecution's line of questioning, that the Croatian government was doing all of these things? This is a Tribunal of individuals. We don't have countries here, but I think this is something that needs to be taken into consideration. Now, I understand the joint criminal enterprise, it has individuals. We're talking about Tudjman, we're talking about -- they're not here to answer, and nobody's here to defend them, and Croatia hasn't sought leave to have a representative over here to protect the interests of Croatia, but it puts us in a very difficult position. And I would ask the Trial Chamber to think about this and, perhaps, at some other point have a discussion, because I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I take your point. My conception or my understanding of this line of questioning is that it is all about the credibility of the witness and not about what the moral quality of the actions of the Croat government is, not -- I don't see that, really, as the issue. I only see it as an issue of credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine, because I'm thinking joint criminal enterprise, that's where my mind is racing, and international armed conflict, you know, might be tied into that as well. So that's my concern. I can only defend my client based on what the evidence is there. But now, if we're going to go into what somebody in the government did that we don't even know, and I'm not contesting that those events weren't occurring, because it was rather obvious that something was being leaked, but how do I defend against that, because my client has nothing to do with it and it's not part of the indictment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to follow up in relation to what Mr. Karnavas said. I, personally, hesitated -- I'm waiting for the interpretation. I, personally, hesitated to say anything of that kind, because my client is before us at the moment and I didn't want this to influence on his testimony. I absolutely understand that the Prosecution has the task to put each and every question that concerns Mr. Petkovic's credibility, but to follow up on what Mr. Karnavas said, why put questions -- why interpret Gotovina's words or the words of a participant of a meeting that wasn't attended by Mr. Petkovic? If we want to challenge Mr. Petkovic's credibility, we should then ask him about what he said in the Blaskic or Kordic case. If he said something that wasn't true in Kordic or Blaskic, if he said something different from what he has been saying in this case, then that is what will challenge his credibility as a witness. I don't believe that the objective is primarily to challenge General Petkovic's credibility. It's rather a matter of speaking about a meeting and saying that there was a joint criminal enterprise that was involved. You might think this is legitimate, Your Honours, but we don't believe that this is a legitimate means of examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have our break. It's going to be the only one, and, well, the tapes were just about empty. So we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move forward to another topic at this point. And in your binder, I think toward the front, behind the index, and for all those in the courtroom, under, I think, a green tab, I'm told, there is a table titled "Herceg-Bosna and the HVO." Binder number 1, the same binder that we've primarily been working on.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that number 1 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can't say that I can see from where you -- the Usher can help you -- will assist you, sir, or he has it separately, I guess, in this case. Maybe not, sorry. I will raise certain parts of it with you, sir, and of course we'll be assisted. This is the schedule, there are the documents behind it. We will -- of course, there will be translation. But the point I want to put to you, sir, in introducing this topic, and it goes really back, again, to your testimony in the earlier case, and in Blaskic in particular, as Judge Jorda's name has been mentioned several times this afternoon, and Judge Jorda asked you this question in Blaskic, and you gave the following answer. This is at transcript page 24221-22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: "I have very few questions, General Petkovic, very few questions. I have a political one. I'm saying this so that Mr. Rifkin," the representative of Croatia, "I'm saying this so Mr. Rifkin will be vigilant." And then he says: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, did it have a political objective?" And you answered: "No, it did not have one, and I did not attend a single meeting of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna." And, sir, I'm putting to you and we're going to talk for some -- probably some time, once again, sir, your answer, under oath, in response to Judge Jorda, was fundamentally false and misleading, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Everything we've covered so far in the cross-examination, sir, your role, your extremely high level and role, far beyond being a soldier, to being a politician, which you, yourself, had indicated you felt more like a politician than a soldier, your involvement in government meetings, your involvement in meetings with Mr. Tudjman, you knew full well what the political programme of Herceg-Bosna was, and when you answered Judge Jorda, No, you testified falsely, didn't you ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are you on your feet, Ms. Alaburic? Is there a problem in the question, a mistake in the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to intervene with regard to a false claim in the question, that the witness felt he was more a politician than a soldier, because Mr. Scott is quoting an introduction to an interview shown yesterday. Those were the words of a journalist. They weren't the words of General Petkovic. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the journalist was reporting on the conversation with Mr. Petkovic, in which Mr. Petkovic, according to the journalist, made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at this document, I'm going to start with -- and I can't go through all of these because, again, we don't have enough time, but, sir, if you'd look down -- if you'd look at item number 1, Exhibit P0079, item number 2, P00151, these are the documents -- some of the documents establishing Herceg-Bosna and Croatia, and they all talk about Croatia this and Croatia that. The first article, P0079, talks about the territories. We see the list of territories claimed. We hear about the seat of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna being in Mostar. We see the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council, the sovereignty of the territories of the Croatian Community, to protect the Croatian people. Sir, if there was no political objective or if this was just motivated by loyalty to and protection of Bosnia-Herzegovina in general, why the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, why the Croatian Defence Council? Why not All People's Defence Council? Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that you have used the term "territory," but we have had many objections because of that. It is "podrucje," which probably false to be translated as "area," and I think it would be better to avoid unnecessary and repetitive discussions about that. So I think it would be a good idea if you used that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But my point remains, sir. Why Croatian this and why Croatian that? Why did you have to rename the university in Mostar the Croatian university? Why change the name of Prozor to Rama? Why change the name Gornji Vakuf to Uskopje, if there was no political objective?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no political objective such as you interpreted. I didn't refer to any political objectives. Could you please precisely quote my answer to the Judge's question? Perhaps we could have a look at what the Judge asked me when I testified, because I don't have my testimony in front of me and I wouldn't like to speak off the top of my head. So could we take that as our starting point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The starting point, sir, is what I read to you, and I'll read it to you again. Judge Jorda asked you this question: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, did it have a political objective? "A. No, it did not have one."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it a political objective or a political programme? Which term was used in the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A political objective, sir. It did, didn't it? Herceg-Bosna had plenty of political objectives, and you knew it. That's what you were fighting for.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political objective of Herceg-Bosna was to protect the Croatian people and others in areas where the Croats were in a majority, and also in areas where they were in a minority. So it had to do with engaging all the Croats to defend themselves against an act of aggression, and that was the sole purpose of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you were acting to protect everyone, sir - I go back to my question before - then why Croatian Defence Council, why Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Why not All People's Defence Council, for example? I'm not going to repeat all my questions to you three or four times, but I have asked you this now. So why, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should ask those who, on the 18th of November, took that decision. I was far away from Herceg-Bosna on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were there at the Presidency meeting in July 1992, when the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was amended. You confirmed that yesterday. You were there, you spoke, you participated. So don't pretend that you don't know. It doesn't help you, sir. It doesn't help to you pretend things that you don't know when you know that you do. You went to work for these people. You worked for Bruno Stojic, you worked for Mate Boban. You knew what their political objectives were, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to item number 3, let's go to item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered the question. I said that the political objective was to protect the Croats and everyone else in the area, and that has been recorded. It was recorded at that meeting that I attended. You can read that. Nothing else was written. The areas of certain municipalities that constitute the HZ-HB were protected, and the possibility of everyone else joining up was there. It wasn't a territorial definition. Anyone who wanted to join could join.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did it say, sir, in the establishment of the HVO, in item number 3, P00154, that the Croatian Defence Council will have exclusive supreme command of the Herceg-Bosna armed forces, that this body is the only legal body, the only legal military, that all other military formations in the area of Herceg-Bosna, the alleged or so-called area of Herceg-Bosna, are illegal or enemy formations? Sir, that doesn't sound to me like the language of someone who's trying to reach out and be inclusive of everyone, but to be quite the contrary, to be exclusive and to exclude, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Read out the first sentence. You skipped that deliberately. You do that whenever you refer to this document. If you do read out the first sentence, you'll see that it says that the Croatian units and Croatian soldiers can only be in the HVO and in no other units. And then there's a criticism of Izetbegovic wanting the TO, but no one is preventing Izetbegovic from having his TO. Here, it is said that the Croats who are organising themselves can only be called the HVO, be part of the HVO. You can't claim what you are claiming, that no one else is legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not what it says at all. That's not what it says at all. It purports to establish the exclusive and only legal armed force on the so-called area or territory of Herceg-Bosna. It doesn't say anything about recognising that, well, the Muslims or the BiH Army can have its units too. It's, No, absolutely not, this is Herceg-Bosna, and the only legal army is going to be the HVO, and everybody else is the enemy. That's what it says, isn't it -- doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the army of the Croats, no, that's not correct. No, that's not what it says here. Read out the first sentence. Allow me to do so, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Since the start of the aggression on the Croatian territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there has been inconsistency in the use of the name for the Croatian forces in Herceg-Bosna." This means that there are problems because the Croats, who organised their army, use several terms. They say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why the Presidency of the Croatian Community took a decision on the 8th of April, 1992, that the supreme body of Croatian defence in Herceg-Bosna should be called the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. So in this document, it says that the Croats, who are organising themselves, can organise themselves as part of the HVO. If the Croats organise themselves into some other unit, this won't be accepted by the HVO, or the Main Staff will not accept them as such. They won't be allowed to be an integral part of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it doesn't say that at all. It doesn't say that at all. Specifically --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, please, please. Mr. Scott is in charge. You can stop the witness, but you should not talk both at the same time, because it's like if no one were speaking. It's only noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. My apologies to you, and my apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, Mr. Petkovic, I don't need to be counselled --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Prosecutor. If you're going to ask him to interpret, and he's giving an interpretation, then have you to allow him to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that's what he was doing. Now, maybe if the question is rephrased in a closer fashion, you know, you can cut him off. But the way the question was phrased, he was answering that question, and there lies the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, he asked me to read something, and I said he could read it, but I'm not going on for five minutes. And you know and I know that we're all operating under severe time-limits, so I cannot allow -- with respect and courtesy to Mr. Petkovic, I cannot allow him to sit here and let him read for 10 minutes, which -- in a non-responsive way, ultimately. I wish that maybe it was otherwise, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this -- Mr. Boban, in this document, responds very specifically. In the second paragraph, he rejects the action of the Presidency in accepting the Bosnian state armed forces: "The decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is politically expedient," et cetera, and he goes on. He's specifically reacting to the establishment of the state armed forces, and Boban is saying, Absolutely not, we will have no part of it. The only legal armed force on the territory or on the area of the so-called Herceg-Bosna is going to be the HVO. Everyone else is illegal and the enemy. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The Croats can --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... didn't ask you for any other answer. Stop. You've answered the question, sir. You said, No. That's your position. Then I'm directing your attention to item number 5 in the table, and P00185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I'm very confused regarding the last paragraph in this document. It is stated there that apart from the HVO, there cannot be any other formation, because any such formation would be illegal. So I'm asking myself, What about the 4th Corps, what about the 1st Mostar Battalion, what about the embryonic ABiH? If we are to read this paragraph in a strict fashion, well, it could be that it was poorly crafted, or does this translate the will to have nothing else but the HVO? That's the question, isn't it? And you have to shed some light on this, even if you did not write this document, yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, my starting point is that Mr. Boban said that when the Croatian forces were organising themselves in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the term to be used was "the HVO." In his opinion, the Croats shouldn't use any other term. If they were to use a different term, the Main Staff wouldn't accept them as their own men. And it says that the Main Staff only accepts those Croatian units that are called the HVO. The Main Staff will not accept the HOS or any other unit formed by Croats, and that is what is at stake here, that's the problem. The ABiH or the TO can establish or organise itself. No one prevented the formation of these units. In Mostar, you saw that a month and a half later, I wrote to Vakuf and Konjic and said that the TO and the HVO were the same armed force, so this -- there's an attempt to interpret this erroneously. The TO wasn't attached to the Main Staff. Units that had been formed by Croats were linked to the Main Staff, and Croats would only recognise the HVO as an organisation, and no other organisation. So that is the substance of this order issued by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was right in asking you this question, because you answered that this text does not prevent the ABiH from being created, but it should be read only through the HVO units. Is this what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't prevent that. Mate Boban, Your Honours, is speaking about the organisation of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina here. The army is established on a principle. The Croats can only organise themselves using the term "the HVO." Boban is not prepared to accept Croat organisations in any other form, as part of the Main Staff. Therefore, it was possible for there to be some other Croatian unit, but he said, I won't accept that, and you won't have ties to the Main Staff. Mate Boban in no way prevented Mr. Izetbegovic from establishing the Territorial Defence in the manner he thought appropriate, and afterwards you can see that there was a TO and an HVO in all municipalities. So how did he prevent this? He didn't do anything to prevent this. Boban quite simply said, and that's in the first sentence, The Croats shall organise themselves within the HVO, and nothing outside of that framework will be accepted. So he is only objecting to Izetbegovic for accepting the TO since it's been compromised, but he's not preventing Izetbegovic from having a TO if he wants it. A few months later, Izetbegovic thought this wasn't a satisfactory state of affairs, so he introduced some changes. In this document, Boban has done nothing to prevent others establishing units of a certain kind. He is addressing Croats, and no one else here. The Croats didn't accept the HOS. Mate Boban didn't want the Croats establishing units of their own that would be called the Territorial Defence. He quite simply didn't want that. If the Croats establish units, they can be called "the HVO." Establish other units in the municipalities, if you like, but you won't fall under the Main Staff, and that is what is at stake. No one is preventing anyone from establishing a Patriotic League, for example, a Territorial Defence, establishing Green Berets, or any other units. Each municipality had a Croatian organisation within the framework of the HVO, and there was an Muslim organisation in the TO, in the Territorial Defence, or in some other formation. They spontaneously established these units. Why would we co-operate with Pasalic in Mostar, for example, if we wanted to implement this? Pasalic organised the Muslims, the Bosniaks. No one prevented him from doing this. But as for the Croats, Boban wanted them to organise themselves within the HVO. If anyone else wanted to form units of another kind, that was fine, but they wouldn't be tied to the HVO. And that is the essence of this document. One has been trying to interpret it as a document that says we're preventing the Presidency from doing certain things. No, that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You took a long time to explain the substance of this document, but it's now been recorded. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on to Exhibit P00185, which is item 5 in the chart. I'm not going to read the entire conversation, but this is a conversation between Mr. Stojic and some of the Serb leadership figures. Maybe you can remind the Chamber who Mico Stanisic is and what role he played in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no idea as to who Mico Stanisic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this conversation, Mr. -- toward the end of the part that's in the table, it says Mr. Stojic refers to -- they're talking about coming to an agreement, and Mr. Stojic says: "There is the 1939 one and none other. I'm dead serious." Stanisic: "We need to see what is realistic there and sit down and make a deal." Stojic: "Only the 1939 borders, and no bargaining. Ha-ha." Now, this is the man, sir, that you described in your previous testimony, and you confirmed here again, this was your minister. This is the man that you said was your superior. This is the man you said was more powerful than you. And you knew, sir, from all your dealings with him in 1992 and 1993, from him and others, that the territorial objectives of Herceg-Bosna, and of Mr. Tudjman, and of Mr. Susak, were to establish -- re-establish the Banovina borders of 1939, weren't they? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Tudjman didn't establish a banovina of any kind in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We look in going to Exhibit -- item 6, P00199. This was an order by Bobetko, which you signed on his behalf, and Boban, appointing the Mostar HVO, appointing Mr. Jadranko Topic and others. By what authority did Mr. -- did a Croatian general, Bobetko, and Mr. Boban -- by what authority did they have to establish the government in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban has the powers to appoint authorities in Mostar. Why he appointed the commanders as listed here is the military aspect, and whereas item 1 refers to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's start --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll come back to Mr. Boban, but let's start with Mr. Bobetko. What authority did the general -- did the head of the Croatian Army, the Republic of Croatia -- what authority did Bobetko have to issue an order appointing the government in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bobetko had no authority to appoint government, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But why is it on this document, sir, and why did you sign for him? Why didn't you say, General, you've asked me to sign this document for you, and surely you have no authority to do this. I'm not putting my name on this because you have no authority to issue such an order, I'm not signing this.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, I was commander, and I had the right to sign that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But what gave you the authority to appoint the government of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was accepted as a member of the HVO, and thus received the authority to sign for the commanding structures. About -- for items 1 and 2, I had no authority over these, but for the following items, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What gave the HVO the authority to appoint the Mostar government?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitutional right of a people to organise itself to oppose an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who gave the HVO the authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a correction of the transcript. I believe that this is very important. This refers to line 6 and 7. General Petkovic said, I had no authority to appoint people under item 1, only Boban could do so, but I did have the authority to appoint those under items 2, 3, 4, et cetera. General, it was recorded in the transcript that you said the following: [In English] "About -- for items 1 and 2, I had no authority over this, but for the following items, I did." [Interpretation] Tell us what you actually said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that I had no authority over the position in item 1, whereas for the commanders of the municipal staffs, which are items 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, I did have the right to sign because at the time I was in a commanding position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The command of what, sir? Were you still acting, in May of 1992, as a Croatian general, or an HVO officer, or both?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a Croatian general. I was an officer of the HVO. I had been relieved of all my duties in the Croatian Army. You have that document from my personnel file, so you can read it any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what gave the HVO the authority to appoint the Mostar government, or Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO is just another name of the authorities that were established pursuant to the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What authorities, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first there were the election results, and then the authorities chose to call themselves HVO, so this was a continuation of the previously existing authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Certain authorities decided to call themselves the HVO. Mr. Boban was never elected mayor of Mostar. He had no legal authority over Mostar whatsoever. When was there an election? When did the Muslim members of the territory claim to be Herceg-Bosna? When was there a referendum? When was there a free election by which the Muslims said, Yeah, we want to be part of this, we sign up voluntarily? Tell me -- give me the date, and where those polling booths were, and where that election was held.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't speak about elections during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You just did.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war had started. The elections were before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. You said, in paragraph -- you said, in page 66, page 66, line 8 and 9: "The HVO is just another name of the authorities that were established pursuant to the elections."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, but not during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was Mr. Boban elected to be the president of Herceg-Bosna, which gave him, according to you, apparently, the authority to appoint the government in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that the central authorities didn't function --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question. Tell me when he was elected?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Boban organised provisional authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell me when he was and by what process he was elected and given this power.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban was provisionally elected president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By who? By who, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I got there, by the representatives of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the representatives of the Croatian people. But you didn't answer the question I put to you five minutes ago, sir. When did the Muslim people who lived within the borders that Herceg-Bosna claimed, when they said, Our borders go all the way to Vares, and our borders go all the way to Gornji Vakuf, and our borders go to Grude, and Stolac, and Mostar, and Jablanica, and Konjic, when did all the Muslims living in those borders -- when were they given the opportunity to vote and say, We freely choose to be part of this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims, as far as I know, accepted the provisional authorities of the HVO in those areas, and they co-operated with each other. They knew that the central authorities didn't function and couldn't function.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They co-operated. Is that why they --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible to establish provisional authorities in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- were rounded up on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, and put in the Heliodrom, because they co-operated and went along? Is that why all the Muslim men, in July 1993, were arrested and put in prisons, because they went along?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was speaking about 1992 now. Many things happened before 1993. Do tell me when the central authorities organised elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir. You're answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in these areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're answering my questions, and you can't presume that the HVO just somehow sprung into existence with legitimacy. It was simply self-declared by a certain group of people who were acting to create their own state, sir, a Croatian state. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no state of any kind. There was a need to organise oneself and defend oneself against the aggression that had already begun in those areas, only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to item 8 in the table, P00279. This is a report, and this is your own document. This is a report that you wrote to the municipal leaders and commanders of the HVO units. And you say, in number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the last document, General Petkovic, I must tell you that I have a question mark when I see the name of Bobetko in it. There are several assumptions we can make. It's a typo, it was your name that should have been there, and "Bobetko" was put in there instead. That's a possibility. Second assumption: There's an agreement between Mate Boban and Bobetko, as far as all these appointments are concerned, and you, who are at the HVO Main Staff, since it is written here, you signed this. That's a possibility. I don't know. If I look at the names of the people who have been appointed, Mr. Topic is seemingly a civilian. I don't see why he would be appointed to a civilian position unless one holds that the president of the HVO in Mostar is a military position. That's also a possibility. I don't know. Jaganjac, commander. From what I understood, this would come under Mr. Boban's authority. If that is the case, why would your signature be needed in that case? What I'm interested in is this: Why is Bobetko mentioned in this document? What business does he have to be there? The Trial Chamber will have to draw its conclusions. Why is his name in this document, and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whoever drafted this document for Mr. Boban obviously didn't know what this was about. The -- General Janko Bobetko was never commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, but somebody wrote it that way. Mr. Boban didn't want it changed, and I signed it because, well, after all, I had accepted a commanding function in the HVO. Why this unknown person put General Janko Bobetko's name under the heading "Commander of the Main Staff of the HVO," I don't know. There's no reason for mentioning Bobetko here, because he never called himself or proclaimed himself commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. I placed my signature there. It would have been better if we had removed that, but such were the times. Anyway, this is my signature, not General Bobetko's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So by way of an explanation, you are telling us that this was a mistake and that you didn't correct it. It's as if someone asked me to sign a judgement, and it says Ms. Alaburic -- stating that Ms. Alaburic is a judge, and then I sign because it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly, but I don't think anybody would like to go back to those times. It would have been important to remove that, but it didn't happen, so it remained. Mr. Boban thought it sufficient for me to sign it as it was, and I signed. But Mr. Bobetko was never the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it had stated at the bottom of the document "General Colin Powell," would you have signed, all the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not, but because that man wouldn't have been there. And, Your Honour, this is the 10th of May, 1992. There is no document that regulates any kinds of relations in the HVO, and yet such documents are drafted. That was the problem, that the HVO had not yet adopted any decrees, laws, regulations, nothing. All we had was an order dated the 10th of April which is half a page long. The relations were not clear, but it was important to appoint people to commanding functions -- to commanding positions and organise the defence of Mostar. And we can't compare this with Colin Powell or anybody else. This was done a month after the fighting at Kupres, and the risk of having half Mostar occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we were about to go to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We were about to go to P00279, line 8 in the table. This is your report, sir, and, among other things, you say, on -- in a number of items, you say: "To put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities." Number 3: "To establish Croatian rule over all municipalities. "Our intentions are, among other things, to prepare ourselves, and through offensive activities, liberate the remaining Croatian territory or area." But, in any event, "to liberate the Croatian area or territory." Now, if this was just one big happy family, all for one, one for all, why didn't you just say "to liberate all of Bosnia and Herzegovina"? Why just "the Croatian area"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did liberate Bosnia and Herzegovina, part of it. The introductory part was drafted by somebody who lived there, unlike me, but that doesn't mean that we claimed all of Bosnia-Herzegovina or part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to ourselves. We always acted in accordance with the principle that it was the common country of Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, why didn't you say that, then? Why didn't you just say that? Why did you say "the Croatian municipalities," "to establish Croatian rule over municipalities," "to liberate the Croatian areas"? It's very simple, sir, and in response to the questions -- answers you just made to the President and questions -- answers to my questions, you can't say, sir, every time that, well, Someone else drafted the document, they weren't your words, and it was all a mistake, and now you wish you had said otherwise. This is your document. It's very easy to say. You're an educated man. You're a professional soldier. You could have very easily said, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. You could have very easily said, Let's put under -- let's put under -- let's get the Serbs out of here, let's re-establish the Bosnian authorities in this area, let's liberate the remaining territory of BiH. There are all sorts of things you could have said that are far more inclusive, but it was "Croatian, Croatian, Croatian." Now, why did you say that? And I remind you, sir, that we started this topic because you told Judge Jorda, under oath, that Herceg-Bosna didn't have a political objective. Why "Croatian, Croatian, Croatian"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipalities mentioned here are Neum, Ravno, Ljubuski, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, and they are purely Croatian municipalities. In others, the Croats are the majority. That's why they're called Croatian municipalities. And they were ruled by the HDZ, and that's what they were called. The second thing here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's go to another [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is part of the area of the Ravno municipality. Let me just explain. In part of the Ravno municipality, which is almost exclusively Croatian because the Croats are the absolute majority there, but a part of it was still not liberated. In the Stolac municipality, there was an area called "Stjepan Kriz," by which name we can judge its nature --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to cut --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am cutting you off now, sir, sorry. If we go back to article -- let's go back to line 1, or P00079. Look at the list of municipalities there, page 1, row 1: "Kakanj, Gornji Vakuf, Konjic, Jablanica, Stolac." Those are all Muslim-majority municipalities. Those aren't Croat majorities at all. Mostar has a Muslim plurality.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's simply false, what you said a moment ago. It's simply false what you said, these were Croat majority -- just the Croat-majority municipalities. They weren't at all, were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the municipalities Neum, Ravno, Capljina, Ljubuski, to the greatest part, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, these are the municipalities I'm talking about, not Kakanj. And I'm speaking about the remainder of the municipality of Stolac and part of the municipality of Ravno, which were yet unliberated. And those were areas mostly inhabited by Croats, and that's why we said that we must --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's stop there --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I believe there is a misunderstanding between Mr. Scott and the witness, because Mr. Scott spoke about a document that we see on our screens, whereas the witness is referring to another document, P279, and that's why they are talking about different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, 079 has nothing to do with this report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Regardless of which list you look at, sir, regardless of which of the lists you look at, you know full well that there were a number of the municipalities claimed by Herceg-Bosna, and we're going to get there in just a moment, we're going to get there. But you know full well that there were a number of these municipalities that weren't Croat-majority municipalities at all; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to your -- so you answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and nobody in the HVO disputed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'll see. And then let's go back to the position you said just a moment ago, because there's really two separate things now going on. You said, Well, we were trying to establish Croatian control in these particular municipalities, these were the Croatian municipalities. Well, there again, sir, what difference did that make? Why did you only want to establish control in certain municipalities and liberate certain municipalities, but not others?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you cannot liberate everything in one operation. Have you to start with one part and proceed to the second, third, fourth, et cetera. So it wasn't possible to conduct operations in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO did what it could, based on its capabilities, so they liberated areas that had -- that previously hadn't been liberated. If you want -- you seem to want us to have liberated all of Bosnia-Herzegovina at once. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not at all what I said. Let's go to the next document. Let's go to line 9, 1D01670. And as we go into this, and I refer you to your participation, we talked yesterday about how you had participated in this meeting. This is a meeting at the HZ-HB Presidency. This is the same meeting where the Decree on Armed Forces was adopted. This is the same meeting where the declaration of the existence of Herceg-Bosna was amended and approved, and you participated in it. And before I put the next statement to you, I remind you and I remind the courtroom of what you said a few moments ago, Well, the Muslims went along. It was okay, it was okay with the Muslims. Well, let's see what you said, sir, in July 1992. Page 4, item 10. Page 4, item 10. Petkovic: "Relations between the Muslims and Croats are poor in the better part of the territory. Efforts have to be made to return the situation to normal. We are the ones who did all this, and they," referring obviously in the context to the Muslims, "are the minority ethnic groups in these parts." You go on to say: "Care must be taken to avoid territorial fragmentation." Well, again, sir, it's simply not true that the Muslims were the ethnic minority in all of those parts. It's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see where you're reading from. Can item 10 be enlarged so that I can read it? I'm saying that outside the area of HZ-HB, adequate resistance isn't offered to the aggressor. That's a statement. Unfortunately, I don't know the balance of forces, but in Eastern Bosnia, one area is falling after another. And then I go on to say the relations between Muslims and Croats in the better part of the territory are poor. Efforts must be made to normalise the condition. We are the ones who did all this, and they are the minority people in these areas. The burden of defence was shifted to municipalities in the outskirts, whereas the others are acting as in peacetime. The line on the Neretva is not safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're not going to read the entire document. I'm sorry we're not going to do that, we're not going to [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't know where --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe the Chamber can give additional time, but we're not simply going to start reading documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, and in reference to the last document we looked at in line 8 of the table, and now in line 9, you repeatedly, sir, are talking about what you're interested in and what the Herceg-Bosna and HVO authorities are interested in is establishing Croatian rule over the so-called Croat municipalities, which you said -- which you say were Croat municipalities or Croat majorities; isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the municipalities I mentioned, as far as I know, are -- have a majority-Croat population, and some of them have 100 per cent of Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can shift to Sanction, please, and we have map 9 from the book of maps, which is marked as Exhibit P09276. The book is P09276. Map number 9. Sir, Kakanj is Muslim majority; Gornji Vakuf is Muslim majority; Konjic is Muslim majority; Jablanica is Muslim majority; Travnik is a Muslim plurality; Bugojno is a Muslim plurality; Konjic is a Muslim plurality; Mostar, itself, is a Muslim plurality; Stolac is a Muslim plurality. Those aren't Croat-majority municipalities at all, are they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the Croats didn't take the entire municipality with them and joined it to the Herceg-Bosna. The HVO wanted to join the Herceg-Bosna, and if the Muslims didn't want that, well, they would remain in their municipality and go on living there. The HVO didn't take away the territory from a certain municipality and take it to Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, they could go on -- the Muslims could go on living there if they accepted HVO control and Herceg-Bosna control. Sure, they could continue living there. We're going to be the masters, we're going to control the government, it's going to be our army, it's going to be our taxes. Yeah, they can continue living there under your terms. Isn't that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are not putting it properly. Take a look at who had the authorities. In Konjic, there was the Crisis Staff, in which the HVO, Croats and Muslims, are participating. Wasn't there in Jablanica a Crisis Staff manned by Croats and Muslims? In Kakanj, there was also a Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the HVO in municipality after municipality was throwing the Muslims out of the authorities. They were just like the document we saw 40 minutes ago. They created the Mostar government, Bobetko -- you signing for Bobetko, and Boban saying, Here's the Mostar government, as we see it. We don't want -- well, you know, the Muslims, well, you know, you can go do your own thing maybe, but this is our government and we're in charge, and this is our army, and it's the only legal one. That's how it was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that wasn't so. We can analyse the authorities in any municipality. There were Crisis Staffs in which there were both Croats and Muslims. What is being put forth here is a construction. Let's take Jablanica or Konjic. There were Crisis Staffs manned by Croats and Muslims. We had a witness from Jablanica and from Konjic, Muslims who were in Crisis Staffs. HVO is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, sir -- if that's the case, then we're jumping ahead of ourselves. But when we get to March and April of 1993, and you say, Well, the Muslims, yeah, they had the right to control their own fate, then why is it -- why do you blame and resist -- why does the HVO resist the Muslims in Konjic and say, Oh, they started the war in Konjic, and it's terrible because the Muslims aren't doing what we want them to do? According to you, the Muslims have every right not to do what the HVO wanted them to do, and they did, didn't they? I came back to what I put to you 45 minutes ago, sir. When did the Muslims vote for Herceg-Bosna? And you never did answer that question, by the way. When did the Muslims vote for Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croats didn't vote for Herceg-Bosna either. You don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, sir. No one elected Boban -- no one elected Boban, or Prlic, or Kordic, or Bender, or Boras. No one elected them legitimately to any of these positions. Power was taken and seized and asserted, with the help of the Government of Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, no. I said that no elections were held, but the representatives of the Croatian people and the authorities under the municipalities organised provisional authorities in that way. And don't talk to me about Konjic and other municipalities, where there was participation in power. Nobody had seized power. The HVO existed in Konjic and participated in power, and then Mr. Cibo comes along and blows everything apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that if we have time, sir. Why Croatian symbols? Why Croatian -- why a flag that looks almost identical to the Croatian flag ? Why insignia and badges that look almost the same as the Croatian Army? Why the Croatian university? You never answered my question. Why Rama instead of Prozor, why Uskopje instead of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before he answers, on the Croatian University of Mostar, and I stand to be corrected and I welcome the opportunity, but we haven't seen a single document where it says that that university was changed from the name that it had to Croatian University of Mostar. It was University of Mostar. And I invite any member of the Bench or the Prosecution, or anyone on the planet, to show me where in the record is a document that states that. So let's be accurate. Now, everything else Mr. Scott is entitled to put, but let's be accurate with the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As to the -- Your Honour, Mr. Karnavas, I won't persist at the moment in that, because I don't want to take the time to do it. I will search for and I believe I can produce that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But in the interests of time, in the interests of time, take Croatian University out of it. Why Croatian symbols, why Croatian insignia, why Croatian flag, why the Croatian national anthem, if this was a territory and area for everybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- Your Honour, again similar objection. I don't remember that ever anybody mentioned "Croatian anthem."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's been played before in court --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- and I will find the exhibit. And I will find the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but not the anthem. The national songs people were singing there for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I disagree with counsel on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, in any event, why Croatian symbols --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Anthem is something in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why Croatian symbols, why all these insignias? We can do this all afternoon, if that's what people want to do, but my question remains to you, sir: Why all these things that were Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, again, they're not Croatian, they're indigenous. These are for Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the importance, not Croatia proper, the Republic of Croatia. We're talking about symbols that the Croats of that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these are their national -- there is a distinction, and keep in mind that we are dealing with constituent peoples. That's the important aspect of this. It may not be important to an American, because we don't have that notion in the United States, but in this part of the world, for better or for worse, it exists, and these are symbols that are designed for those people living there, not from some other country. So if we're going to be accurate, let's be accurate and then pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think Mr. Karnavas needs to be testifying and telling us which -- what the source of these are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, perhaps you should highlight with your question, if it's possible, a difference between the local symbols, Croatian symbols, from Croatian symbols. I think what you have in mind are those symbols that relate directly to the Republic of Croatia. Maybe that's what the issue hinges on. Through your questions, he might say that he agrees or disagrees with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if need be. After almost four years of trial, I think everyone should be familiar, all of us, with some of these things. But if it's necessary, by Monday I'll try to bring in a picture of the Croatian flag and a Herceg-Bosna flag, and the HV badge and the HVO badge, and the songs that were sung, and the Croatian names, and the name of the university. I'll try to bring all those in, if that's what it's going to take. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, in the interests of time, you know that we've seen documents in this courtroom. What do you say? You've heard Defence counsel making points, presenting submissions. You've heard the Prosecutor's question. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those aren't the symbols of the Republic of Croatia. They are the symbols of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They used them even at the time of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They had such a flag at that time, and they kept it. And the flags are not the same. The sequence of the colours, red, white and blue, doesn't mean that the flags are the same. The flag of the Republic of Croatia differs from that of Herceg-Bosna. And the military insignia were also different. We had insignia saying "HVO," so I don't see where that similarity is. It was completely different, and we cannot say that something is similar if it isn't. I cannot say that Mr. Scott resembles Mr. Stringer because they are both Prosecutors, because they are different. And along the same lines, the flag of Herceg-Bosna is not the same as that of Croatia. All these symbols and insignia were those of Herceg-Bosna. I removed all my insignia and placed HVO insignia instead. So there were differences between the symbols. They were the symbols of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, all right. You've just said it. These are the -- it's on line -- sorry, that's what I was trying to do, Mr. President. I'm sorry. Page 82 of today's transcript, line 13: "All these symbols and insignia were those of Herceg-Bosna." Well, that's exactly the point. They were the symbols and insignia of Herceg-Bosna. These were the symbols you said a few moments ago of the Croatian people, but how about the symbols of the Muslim people, the indigenous symbols, as it was referred to a few moments ago? Why did you pick -- why did the HVO -- why did Herceg-Bosna pick only the Croatian symbols? Why didn't you have a flag with a chequer-board on it and a lily? Why didn't you call it the All People's Defence Council? Why Croatia -- the same question, sir, that I've been asking for the past hour. Why "Croatia, Croatia, Croatia," if there was no political objective, as you told Judge Jorda?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not our political goal. It was an impetus for the Croats to organise and defend Bosnia and the areas where they lived. If no commander in Tuzla minded having an HVO brigade with Croatian insignia, why would anyone have minded?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, they did mind, sir. They did mind. They did mind. Maybe not in Tuzla, when they put themselves under the local -- under the authority of the national government, but in Herceg-Bosna they did. The Muslims kept telling you over and over again. Izetbegovic kept telling you over and over again, We're not buying it -- well, we'll get to those. Throughout -- through a number of the meetings, including the so-called friendship meeting, Mr. Izetbegovic and others tell Mr. Tudjman over and over again, We don't accept Herceg-Bosna. And if anyone wants to read one transcript, and I believe it's P00336, read it. Read it four times, because Mr. Izetbegovic tells Tudjman and the others, over and over again, We don't accept Herceg-Bosna, we're not joining, we're not on board. And we'll get to those documents on Monday or Tuesday, if we have time. Sir, you know full well that when you describe something as Croatian, such as "Croatian Mostar," the implication is -- the meaning of that -- the connotation is that it is Croatian and nothing else, that Croatians are in charge, Croatians are in control, Croatia -- it's Croatia, and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. Croats and Muslims in those areas, starting with Southern Mostar and all around Mostar, were together, and they did not mind. They crossed the Neretva together, and they didn't mind being in the HVO and the HVO being called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They might not have in May of 1992, but they did soon thereafter. You said in your own report, a few minutes ago -- we looked at it, and you said relations between the Muslims and Croats by July of 1992 were in most parts poor, and you said it the other day. Let's go to slide 22, please, in Sanction. This is your testimony on the first day, sir: "As for the term "Croatian,' if anybody said 'Croatian Mostar,' of course, that could be understood to mean that no Muslims are there." You gave us your definition of what that meant on the very first day of your testimony under oath. There it is. If something is called "Croatian Mostar," that means no Muslims are there. And that's what you meant when you said "Croatian territory," "the Croatian Army," "the Croatian government," "the Croatian republic," "the Croatian HVO." That's what you meant, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's incorrect. The Muslims were there, and they lived together with Croats, and they fought together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Line 13 in the table, P00307, the Book of Service Rules. These are the service rules of the HVO, the army of which you were the commander. Page 1, a part of the -- a part of the objectives and strategy of -- or the goals of bringing young men into the Croatian Army of Herceg-Bosna: "Develop love for and loyalty to HZ-HB. "The independence and territorial integrity of the HZ-HB. "To protect and defend the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of HZ-HB." Again on number 3: "To protect and defend the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the HZ-HB." Number 8, continuing to the top of -- or it's in the same row, excuse me: "The independence and integrity of the HZ-HB." Not Bosnia, not Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the territorial integrity of Bosnia, not the independence of Bosnia, not the sovereignty of Bosnia, but the HZ-HB. That's what you were fighting for, isn't it -- wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HZ-HB in Bosnia. We were the majority army, and we had initiative over the Serbs at the time. We were defending our parts, whereas the Army of B and H were defending Eastern Bosnia and the Tuzla Corps area. Therefore, we were defending the HZ-HB, and thus were defending Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You weren't the majority army, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, indeed, managed to defend it wherever our troops were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You weren't the majority army. We went through -- we looked at the map a few minutes ago. There are all sorts of municipalities within the HZ-HB that were not Croat at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. I said where we fought the Serbs, that's where we were in the majority. I did not mean to dispute the fight of the Muslim people, be it by themselves or alongside us. In these areas, we put up fierce resistance to the Serb aggression, and thanks to that we kept the area, and thus we preserved Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had we not managed to defend it in the southern part, it's highly questionable as to what would have happened with it until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to line 14 -- let's go to line 14 or row 14, P00588. This is from the Decree on Armed Forces . Article 21 says: "The HZ-HB Armed Forces shall protect the sovereignty of HZ-HB and defend its territorial integrity." Article 86 establishes the oath, and we've heard this oath in the courtroom. We saw the video of the swearing-in ceremony in Zenica, or around Zenica, the Jure Francetic Brigade, and we saw -- I believe Mr. Kordic was there, and I think Mr. Praljak was there, and we heard the HVO soldiers taking the oath. And what the oath says is, as indicated here: "I shall protect and defend my motherland of Herceg-Bosna, its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and all its citizens." Not Bosnia, not the motherland of Bosnia, not the sovereignty of Bosnia, not the territorial integrity of Bosnia, but Herceg-Bosna. That was the oath that HVO soldiers had to take, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the oath, but it did not negate the notion of Bosnia-Herzegovina; quite to the contrary. We were a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we waited for the Presidency of the B and H to forward an oath that we could use, but nothing of the sort took place in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're not serious -- you're not serious about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was Bosnia -- it was the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was their fault that they didn't send you a different oath? You really want us to take that seriously, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me, what did the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever send to the Croats? Let's see Alija Izetbegovic's document and how he tried to implement the Zagreb Agreement with the Croats. Let's discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They offered you, sir -- they offered you membership in --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- the joint armed forces. They offered you, and we'll get there eventually, and again if we have time, we'll go through the documents, and they said, You want to be part of us, you can join us. We're happy to have you, but you become part of this armed forces, under our command, and of course the HVO would have no part of it, would they? No, they didn't?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, an ancillary question. Did you take an oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina temporarily. There was no need for me to take the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I'm looking at this document presented by Mr. Scott. There may have been a problem. If you wanted to protect your motherland of Herceg-Bosna, this was not your mother country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not my mother country, but I put myself at the disposal to others to help them in defending the areas where they lived. A mother country or a homeland is a narrower concept to me. Dalmatia, for example, could be my homeland. By creating our community there, we did not try to disrupt Bosnia-Herzegovina, as such. We waited for their government to sit down and start regulating matters, some of which they never did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, now you know that you did not take this oath. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following up on this, sir, I want to go back to something that Judge Trechsel put to you on the first day of your testimony, on the 11th of February, because it really rings true, at least to me. It resonates again today of what you've been telling us all afternoon. Judge Trechsel said: "Mr. Petkovic, listening to you, one gets the impression that it was a matter of course that the authorities would be Croat, but that may be the issue, to establish Croat rule even where previously, as in Stolac, there was not a Croat rule, and even a clear Muslim majority in the population. I think that was the point that the President," referring to a question by the President, "was raising here." And I put it to you -- and I adopt that question or that comment and I put it to you again. The problem, if I can put it to you this way, sir, what your position is, you just presume that there was some sort of legitimate claim of these HVO authorities springing into existence and having some sort of legal claim to do everything that it did, and dominate the Muslims, and establish -- and for Bobetko and Boban to appoint the mayor -- the government of Mostar, and to establish which territories and armies they want, with all other armies being illegal. You just presumed that that's the case; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right. I don't know when I presumed that. How come Mr. Izetbegovic had no problem with coming to Zagreb and to sign the Agreement on Co-operation and Friendship? It was all happening early on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, again you take that out --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went there to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say that as if that's all the case, but that friendship agreement, so-called, number 1, says absolutely nothing about -- it came out of the same meeting we were talking about 20 minutes ago, in which Izetbegovic told Tudjman and all those others present, We don't accept Herceg-Bosna, we will not accept Herceg-Bosna. You can see Tudjman getting frustrated with Izetbegovic, but Izetbegovic sticks to his position, We will have nothing to do with Herceg-Bosna. If the HVO, as a military force, wants to put itself under BiH government command, we will accept that happily and we will fight together, but you come join us, you put yourself under our command. We will do that. And you didn't do that, did you, because that wasn't part of the political objective? The political objective was to establish your own little Croat statelet, under your control and with the borders that you wanted. That was the political objective, at least in part, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the objective. We waited for Mr. Izetbegovic to come so that we could continue further elaborating the plan. Why didn't he come? He came to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why didn't you go to him, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to see him at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. He's entitled to answer the question. That was a very long question, with all sorts of predicates. He's not entitled to do that and then cut the witness off. It is impolite, and it is unethical, in my opinion. Now, he should be entitled to answer that question, even if it's going to take a little bit of his time. Otherwise, go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to do that, sir. He said -- I'll take it -- his answer is -- his attitude towards it is, Why didn't Izetbegovic come to us? And I accept that as his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's go to exhibit -- line 24 --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to row 24 of the table, P01032, and this is a video. And I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can set -- get that ready to present, please. This is the video of the session -- of the meeting of the Presidency on the 28th of August, 1993, where the Croatian Republic, not the Community, but the Croatian Republic was established. And among others, Your Honours, I'll watch -- and some of it goes very quickly, but if you watch very carefully, you'll see Mr. Petkovic there, you'll see Mr. Boban, you'll see Mr. Prlic. I think you'll see Mr. Stojic. But this is at the meeting of the Presidency on the 28th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Those in favour of the republic ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The booth should have a transcript as well, I believe, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you just saw yourself, didn't you, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go back, please. Go ahead and play it forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you're in the back there, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go back for just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Against the wall there, please, is that you there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's why I asked to see where I was in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it's almost 6.00, and I want to try -- at least I want to try, if I'm able, to finish this particular topic this evening, subject, of course, to questions from the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But as I said -- as I said an hour and a half or so ago, and I put it to you again in closing out this topic, when you sat here in this same building in the Blaskic case, under oath, and when Judge Jorda asked you whether the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had a political objective, and when you said, No, that was not really a very accurate or fair answer, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked about a political programme and not about any objectives, as far as I recall. The programme was, and one could say "objective," to defend those areas from the Serb Chetnik aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's an appropriate place to stop, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we're going to call it a day, but I just have one tiny question. Looking at this, did everybody vote? Did you vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I held no right to vote. Only the delegates who came could vote. I was there as a guest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to ascertain. It's now 6.00. The tape has run to its end, or just about. We shall reconvene, as you know, on Monday at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
